For that, you need its shape. And skew is named for the long tail, not for the peak. A tail to the right drags the mean above the median. A tail to the left drags it below. Symmetric data keeps the two together. Two peaks usually mean two groups in one column. Mix the heights of two groups, and the mean lands in the valley between them. It describes neither group. And the tails matter as much as the middle.

Draw twenty thousand values from a normal distribution, and just one lands beyond four standard deviations. From a heavy-tailed one, a hundred and twenty-seven do. Heavy tails make rare events routine. Financial returns, insurance losses and network delays all live out there. So a value far out isn't automatically a mistake.

An outlier is a value far from the rest. That's all the word means. It might be an error, like a typo. It might be a placeholder, like minus nine ninety-nine for missing. Or it might be real... your biggest customer, or a fraud. Now take two hundred skewed incomes, plus two genuine high earners. The box-plot fences flag six points. The z-score rule flags just two. Four of those six are simply the long tail of ordinary incomes. So a flag is a question, not a verdict. Find out why a point is out there, and then decide. And the surest way to find out is to look.
